A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FakeSTormer research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, algorithms, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial rearrangement.

before.justification: v1 reports original FakeSTormer benchmark results, component ablations, robustness experiments and appendix analyses, including multi-shot inference.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results on DiffSwap and selected DF40 manipulations, alongside additional baseline evaluations.

M1.justification: The SBV synthesis procedure, vulnerability-driven Cutout, modified TimeSformer, auxiliary heads, losses and appendix multi-shot inference procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 confirms procedural continuity despite the SBVs-to-SBV rename and revised descriptions of the synthesis components.

E1.justification: v3 adds diffusion-generated DiffSwap evaluation and three DF40 manipulation subsets: BlendFace, FSGAN and MobileSwap. These extend the represented forgery-generation regimes beyond v1's retained benchmarks. The reported evaluation does not cover all 40 DF40 techniques.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds SBI and LFGDIN; Table 2 adds StA+VB and a TimeSformer+SBV control; Table 4 adds SBI, LSDA, RealForensics, NACO and LFGDIN. These substantially expand comparator membership within corresponding experiments, including retained benchmarks.

E3.justification: Tables 2 and 6 introduce a raw-FF++ (c0) TimeSformer+SBV evaluation configuration. Appendix 6.8 specifies a new DiffSwap test construction using 250 real CDF videos. Existing frame extraction, resolution, video-level AUC, optimization budget and multi-shot procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Component, loss-weight and normalization analyses are extended to DiffSwap, and Table 6 adds a c0-trained SBV baseline alongside c23 configurations. Existing corruption tests, saliency maps, auxiliary-output examples and multi-shot analyses are retained; their relocation does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version discloses repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both retain point AUC reporting. MeanStd target normalization and multiple inference shots are not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New results include 96.9% DiffSwap AUC for c23 training with T=4 (Table 1), and c0-trained scores of 97.7% on DiffSwap and 91.1%, 96.4% and 95.0% on the three DF40 subsets (Table 2). Table 4 adds manipulation-specific scores. Retained per-dataset values are unchanged; revised ablation averages reflect expanded dataset coverage.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(15), derivative construction and computational-complexity reasoning remain mathematically equivalent. Correcting the prose ordering of H and G aligns it with the existing h/g mappings without changing the definitions. No new theoretical results or proofs appear.

C1.justification: v1 presents generalization and interpretability as headline goals. v3 removes interpretability from the title, abstract and contribution list, and elevates robustness to high-quality videos with subtle artifacts into a central objective. Auxiliary-output insights remain, but their role in the claimed contribution is reduced.

C2.justification: v1 explicitly interprets auxiliary outputs as providing interpretability; v3 Appendix 6.6 describes them more cautiously as potentially useful for prediction post-analysis. The explanation of stacked-SBI failure also changes from overfitting spatial artifacts to overfitting more obvious artifacts. Existing computational-cost qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents DiffSwap generation provenance and its 250-video source population, and identifies the MeluXina computing resource. It removes v1's Code Release subsection describing supplementary code, pending licensing and planned pretrained weights. The repository link remains; actual availability changes cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from interpretability toward explicit vulnerability supervision and high-quality artifact detection. A dedicated synthesis discussion distinguishes SBV from STC, VB and ST-SBV, while the introduction contrasts its supervision with LFGDIN/ISTVT's implicit attention. References add newer detectors and benchmarks and remove two interpretability/localization-oriented works.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction and related-work narrative are rewritten. Terminology changes from SBVs to SBV, saliency discussion moves into Section 4.4, auxiliary-output discussion moves into the appendix, and references precede a separately headed supplementary section.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 2-4 are consolidated into v3's four-panel Figure 2. Saliency and auxiliary-output figures exchange main-text/appendix placement while retaining their images. Multiple tables gain dataset, comparator, manipulation or training-status columns, and interpretability columns are removed, substantially revising the presentation.

improvement.justification: Beyond v1's already extensive evaluation, v3 tests newer forgery regimes, adds stronger comparators and a raw-data SBV control, and exposes manipulation-specific performance. The reduced headline emphasis on interpretability better matches the qualitative evidence. These are useful but bounded gains: DF40 coverage includes only three subsets, and broad superiority wording needs qualification given results such as BlendFace AUC of 91.1% versus LAA-Net's 91.2% in Table 2.
